preamble: The debuccalization of the voiceless labiodental fricative /f/ to the glottal fricative /h/ is a classic example of lenition. This shift involves moving the site of friction from the lips and teeth to the glottis. It is famously documented in the transition from Latin to Spanish and also appears in the historical development of Japanese and other language families. Gascon underwent the same change independently: Latin fīlius, ferrum and festa gave hilh, hèr and hèsta [ˈhɛsto].

examples.note: Latin initial f- became [h] in Old Spanish, which later became silent in the modern language.
Initial f- weakening: Latin 'to do' → Spanish 'to do'.
Historical *p underwent lenition to [ɸ] and then [h] in modern Japanese (except before /u/).

languageExamples.language: Proto-Polynesian to Hawaiian / Rapa Nui / Māori

examples.note: Medial *f > h; the initial *f gave Māori w here
Word-initial Latin f became [h], which parts of Gascony then lost ([ˈɛsto]). Other Occitan dialects keep f (filh, fèrre, fam).
